165: out "● How a Lighthouse Works"; out "A lighthouse is a tower that marks a dangerous or important point on the coast so that ships can navigate safely,"; out "especially at night or in poor visibility. Its three main parts are:"; out "- The light source. A lamp, once an oil or gas flame and now usually an LED, produces the beam."; out "- The optic. A system of lenses and prisms, often a Fresnel lens, gathers the light from the lamp and focuses it into"; out "a concentrated beam instead of letting it spread in all directions."; out "- The rotating mechanism. A clockwork or motor turns the optic so the beam sweeps across the horizon. Each lighthouse"; out "has its own flash pattern, so sailors can tell which light they are seeing."; out ""; out "The lamp sits at the center of the optic, and the optic is mounted on a turntable or inside a rotating drum. Its"; out "curved glass panels bend light that would otherwise escape upward or downward into a narrow horizontal band. The"; out "result is a beam that is much brighter at sea than the bare flame would be, and the rotation makes it appear as a"; out "flash rather than a steady glow."; out ""; out "The tower's height matters as well. A higher light can be seen from farther away, because the curve of the Earth"; out "limits how far a light near the water can reach the horizon. Modern lighthouses often run automatically on solar or"; out "mains power, and many now use GPS and radio beacons alongside the light, but the basic principle of a focused,"; out "rotating beam that identifies a location has not changed for about two centuries."; out ""; out "✻ Churned for 4s · done 12:03 PM"; out ""; out "⏵⏵ auto mode on (shift+tab to cycle)"
